entry.title: India's fertiliser subsidy needs reform beyond digital verification
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / India's fertiliser subsidy needs reform beyond digital verificationIndia's fertiliser subsidy needs reform beyond digital verification

The objective should be to improve targeting without making access to an essential agricultural input conditional on the perfection of land records

premium

Allocation for fertiliser subsidies for 2026-27 stands at about ₹1.71 trillion, but expenditure could be substantially higher this year due to higher international prices owing to the West Asia crisis

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 09 2026 | 10:31 PM ISTIn a year when the subsidy bill is expected to increase, the 37.56 per cent reported decline in fertiliser sales in select border districts during the 2026 kharif season has come as a relief, following the introduction of  digital verification of purchases. The decline was registered after linking purchases to farmer IDs, land records, and crop requirements through AgriStack and other digital platforms. The diversion of subsidised urea for industrial use and across borders has been a long-standing concern. The decline in offtake offers a fresh indication of the potential scale of leakage. The price differential is substantial: A 45-kg bag of urea is available to Indian farmers for about ₹265, against an estimated global landed price of ₹1,674 (September). Predictably, the fiscal implications are also significant. Allocation for fertiliser subsidies for 2026-27 stands at about ₹1.71 trillion, but expenditure could be substantially higher this year due to higher international prices owing to the West Asia crisis. Even for 2025-26, expenditure is estimated to have reached ₹2.11 trillion, around 26 per cent above the Budget Estimate of ₹1.68 trillion and 13.4 per cent higher than the Revised Estimate of ₹1.86 trillion.  Against this backdrop, the Framework for Fertiliser Sales (FFS) is a welcome intervention by the Union government. It links the farmer’s digital identity and verified land records with crop requirements before a purchase is completed. Combined with the existing Integrated Fertiliser Management System, the framework can help identify unusual purchase patterns, monitor district-level consumption, and rationalise subsidy distribution. The decline in fertiliser sales in districts covered under the pilot also suggests that the potential benefits extend beyond border areas. However, changes in cropping patterns and lower rain this year also need to be accounted for in the decline in fertiliser sales.  Equally important is ensuring that digital verification does not exclude legitimate cultivators. Tenant farmers, sharecroppers and those cultivating land with incomplete or disputed records may find it difficult to establish their eligibility. Since land ownership and cultivation are not always aligned, linking access too closely to land records may risk making the system less inclusive. The objective should be to improve targeting without making access to an essential agricultural input conditional on the perfection of land records.  More fundamentally, better monitoring alone cannot correct the distortions embedded in India’s fertiliser policy. Urea, the major source of nitrogen (N) remains heavily subsidised, while phosphatic (P) and potassic (K) fertilisers are relatively expensive. This encourages excessive nitrogen application at the expense of other essential nutrients. India’s N:P:K consumption ratio stood at 9.3:3.5:1 in 2024-25 against the commonly cited agronomic benchmark of 4:2:1. The resulting imbalance has implications for soil health, nutrient efficiency, and overall agricultural productivity. The government should also use digital infrastructure not merely to track fertiliser transactions but to move towards a more rational subsidy regime. Gradual price rationalisation, better-designed direct benefit transfers, and stronger incentives for balanced nutrient application can reduce both diversion and excessive fertiliser consumption. Soil-health cards and crop-specific fertiliser recommendations can inform these changes. Potential savings on fertiliser subsidies will enable the government to spend more on growth-augmenting asset creation.     Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment fertiliser subsidy Urea

entry.title: Democrat control of Congress may bring limited gains for India-US ties
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Democrat control of Congress may bring limited gains for India-US tiesDemocrat control of Congress may bring limited gains for India-US ties

To be sure, the Democrats will have the security of a United States Supreme Court judgment of February, which struck down the President's use of emergency powers to impose tariffs on trading partners

premium

India-US trade relations remain in focus amid discussions over tariffs, a bilateral trade deal and immigration policies

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 09 2026 | 10:20 PM ISTWith the Democrats set to take control of Congress in January next year, there is some anticipation that India can expect greater stability and better visibility in dealing with a range of issues impacting Indo-United States relations, chief among them being the long-stalled trade deal, immigration, and the stringent H1B visa regime. Such hopes are not entirely misplaced, although the President retains, and is likely to wield, the considerable executive powers at his disposal for the remaining two years of his term. Beyond these specifics, however, any optimism must be tempered by the realities of political outlooks.   Though the Democrats have not been India’s natural allies in the past, the nation looks forward to the prospect of Congress exerting a more stable influence on tariffs, shielding countries, including India, from Trumpian unpredictability. To be sure, the Democrats will have the security of a United States (US) Supreme Court judgment of February, which struck down the President’s use of emergency powers to impose tariffs on trading partners. But the framework for an interim trade agreement between the US and India, which the two sides decided in February, is yet to yield a formal trade deal that has been in the works since February 2025. Since then, tensions erupted over Russian oil purchases, which caused Mr Trump to impose additional tariffs on India until the verdict of the Supreme Court; fresh tensions over tariffs under a different law over alleged overcapacity and the use of forced labour further vitiated relations. US purchases of Russian diesel to cool domestic gasoline prices also negated Washington’s objections to India’s oil deals with Russia.  Hopes of a speedy conclusion of a trade deal still depend on Mr Trump’s priorities. Even assuming his administration chooses to give India precedence over larger and more consequential trade partners such as China, with whom Washington has signed a temporary trade truce and framework agreement, or Canada, where a tariff dispute is yet to be sorted, Congress could become a potential hurdle. Although all trade deals don’t have to be approved by Congress, it could still question executive decisions and scrutinise such deals under its broad oversight powers. While moderate Democrats still dominate both the Houses, the unprecedented success of the party’s left caucus — with its uber-focus on egalitarian and secular ideals and pro-Palestinian inclination — is likely to influence the direction of policy. In that respect, India’s domestic politics and policies, along with its close alliance with Israel, could be open to greater scrutiny.  The same sociopolitical factors could influence the Democrats’ approach to the H1B-visa programme. Congress sets the statutory caps and limits for the programme. Though the Democrats have been vocal in opposing the enhanced $100,000 fee for the H1B visa (now temporarily blocked by the courts), petitions for relaxation cannot be taken for granted, given that Indians account for over 70 per cent of the H1B applicants and approvals. Overall, the Democrats’ approach to immigration can be expected to mark a significant softening over the current hardline approach under Mr Trump. But given that immigration remains a bipartisan concern, India may not be able to assume significant gains under a Democrat-led Congress.     Topics : Donald Trump India US Trade Deal US Congress immigration

entry.title: Agnipath 2.0 may ease recruitment pressures but weaken defence reform
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Agnipath 2.0 may ease recruitment pressures but weaken defence reformAgnipath 2.0 may ease recruitment pressures but weaken defence reform

Agnipath 2.0 may ease personnel shortages and retain trained soldiers, but higher pay and benefits risk adding to pension costs and squeezing funds for defence modernisation.

premium

Changes to the Agnipath scheme aim to retain trained personnel for longer, but higher salaries and benefits could increase the defence budget burden and affect spending on military modernisation. | Photo: PTI

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 7:18 PM ISTThe Centre’s decision to modify the Agnipath scheme partially reverses the objective for which this recruitment programme for the defence forces was launched four years ago. Introduced following the government’s acceptance of the One Rank One Pension (OROP) scheme for the defence services in 2014, it sought to contain the burgeoning costs of personnel and pension owing to that decision. The original Agnipath scheme offered a four-year term of duty for soldiers below the rank of commissioned officers for all three services, bypassing traditional service benefits such as pension and rations. Those exiting the scheme after four years would be receiving a lump sum payment (Seva Nidhi) and support for future employment after discharge. The initial scheme provided for 25 per cent of Agniveers to be absorbed into the regular services on the basis of merit after the four-year term. An analysis by the Observer Research Foundation suggests that an Agniveer costs the government roughly ₹1.75 lakh less a year than a traditional soldier on standard pay bands. Under the new scheme, the 75 per cent of the Agniveers due to exit have been offered a two-year extension with a sharp pay increase of ₹43,500 and ₹47,500 in the two-year period with an option to enrol as regular soldiers at the end of two years based on their willingness to continue and merit. Those who exit after this two-year extension will benefit from an enhanced government contribution to the Seva Nidhi package from 50 per cent to 70 per cent.  The new scheme seeks to address some immediate issues. First, it would retain combat-trained Agniveers for longer and save on training costs, which will partly offset enhanced outlays under the new scheme. Second, the extension retains Agniveers who would have exited in the ordinary course, partially addressing the problem of both rising youth unemployment and a shortfall in defence personnel following a two-year recruitment freeze during Covid. These are legitimate solutions but the enhanced pay and Seva Nidhi payouts are likely to impose long-term pressures on an already stretched defence budget. The government allocated ₹17,396 crore for the Agnipath scheme in the 2026-27 defence budget, a 58 per cent increase over 2025-26. The new scheme, thus, will add to the bill for salaries and pensions, which already accounts for 44 per cent of the defence budget this financial year, with pensions alone (₹1.71 trillion) accounting for 22 per cent.  The enhanced spending on Agnipath 2.0 is also likely to crowd out defence capital expenditure, especially on modernisation, which is sorely needed to boost the defence forces’ capabilities. Upgrades are urgently needed across the defence services — fighter and transport aircraft, helicopters, warships, submarines and even basic artillery guns, apart from new-age missiles and advanced unmanned aerial vehicles. An unintended consequence of Agnipath 2.0 is also likely to be accentuated — the weakening of the traditional esprit de corps of the regimental system, which relies on shared identity. There is some anxiety that competition for four- and six-year slots could vitiate the camaraderie so essential to combat efficacy. Agnipath 1.0 was launched to address a defence budgetary issue. In seeking to address unanticipated short-term problems, Agnipath 2.0 is likely to weaken the original objective.   Topics : Indian Army BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Army Military spending Indian military

entry.title: Demonetisation, 10 years after: Evidence still points to limited gains
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Demonetisation, 10 years after: Evidence still points to limited gainsDemonetisation, 10 years after: Evidence still points to limited gains

Demonetisation failed to deliver a lasting reduction in cash circulation or clear evidence of black money being unearthed, while causing widespread disruption to businesses and individuals.

premium

A decade after demonetisation, cash circulation in India remains at nearly the same share of GDP as before the 2016 exercise, raising questions over its effectiveness in curbing black money.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 7:13 PM IST“Demonetisation has been a radical, unprecedented step with short-term costs and long-term benefits,” noted the Economic Survey of 2016-17. To be fair, many commentators at that time believed it could have longer-term benefits. But that began to change soon. On November 8, 2016, the government decided to withdraw high-value currency notes of ₹500 and ₹1,000 from circulation. Those constituted about 86 per cent of the currency by value. The basic objective was to attack black money. It was reasoned that the “magnitude of cash in circulation is directly linked to the level of corruption”. The move was part of the overall fight against corruption, counterfeiting, and terrorism. The implicit assumption was that those holding black money would not come forward to exchange or deposit cash due to the fear of getting exposed. The government had taken various other steps to curb black money, such as the 2015 law on disclosing black money and the 2016 law on benami transactions.  In a large economy like India, aggregate outcomes are often difficult to explain by a single factor. In the initial months and years of demonetisation, the government presented data and evidence in terms of an increase in the number of income-tax filings and collection of data that would help track black money and so on. Critics, on the other hand, argued that the lack of currency notes affected small businesses and the unorganised sector disproportionately. The slow pace of remonetisation did create difficulties for businesses and individuals. Sustained long queues in front of banks showed that the system was not prepared for such a large-scale operation.  Now that a decade has passed, and with the benefit of hindsight, it is worth asking whether demonetisation was worth the trouble. The answer clearly is “no”. Most of the demonetised notes came back, and not much has been reported on how much black money was unearthed. Note that it was an attack on high cash circulation, which was seen as a symptom of corruption and illicit wealth. As the data featured elsewhere in this edition shows, cash as a proportion of gross domestic product was roughly at the same level in 2025-26 (12.06 per cent) as in 2015-16 (12.08 per cent). So, nothing changed.  The ratio did go down in 2016-17, partly because of the pace of remonetisation, but it started moving up in subsequent years. In fact, such a level of cash in circulation is more intriguing in 2026 than it was in 2016, given that India now has a popular and efficient digital payments infrastructure. Large volumes of transactions are processed in real time through the Unified Payments Interface (UPI). The level of cash in the economy is also puzzling for the Reserve Bank of India as was recently articulated by one of its top officials. Currency in circulation is growing even as the share of cash in individual transactions is declining. It appears that cash is still preferred for large transactions, possibly to maintain anonymity or avoid taxes. Cash usage in real estate, for instance, is still said to be very high. Clearly, withdrawing about 86 per cent of cash at one stroke hasn’t yielded much. It also made it clear that there is no magic bullet for solving complex economic or social problems. Change usually is a process in a democracy and requires sustained effort and policy management. Reduction in the generation of black money will require a substantial reduction in the presence of the state in economic life, better use of technology to detect tax evasion, and tax reforms at various levels of government.   Topics : Demonetisation BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Banking sector currency notes

entry.title: Green crackers, hazy reality: Allowing these may have only marginal impact
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Green crackers, hazy reality: Allowing these may have only marginal impactGreen crackers, hazy reality: Allowing these may have only marginal impact

Green crackers and restricted timings may do little to ease pollution in the National Capital Region

premium

A child lights a firecracker during Diwali celebrations (Photo: AdobeStock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 11:42 PM ISTThe Supreme Court has negotiated the thin line between popular sentiment and public health and environmental concerns by extending conditional permission for bursting green crackers within a restricted time window on November 7 and 8. At a time when the air-quality index swings between “severe” and “hazardous”, this well-meaning order is unlikely to clear the air around or after Diwali. For one, enforcing these restrictions demands a level of monitoring that is well beyond the capabilities or the inclination of the state police forces or the political administration. Two years ago, the apex court sharply rebuked the Delhi Police for its inability to enforce the cracker ban. It is also doubtful whether the restrictions limiting firecracker sales to products certified by government bodies can be monitored, let alone implemented. Media reports have already tracked hectic clandestine sales of non-green fireworks, which a certain kind of consumer demands because they literally offer more bang for the buck than the green variants do — and are available in elusive popup shops in small lanes. Fake QR codes have also proliferated.     But the genuine health and environmental safety of green crackers themselves remains doubtful. The Supreme Court has stipulated that only crackers certified by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-Neeri) or the Petroleum and Safety Organisation (Peso) and identified with specific QR codes can be sold. Though both CSIR-Neeri and Peso are guaranteed to follow strict standards, the problem lies in the definition of “green cracker”, which may be somewhat misleading. They are said to reduce particulate matter (PM) 2.5 and 10 by some 30 per cent and emit 10 per cent less harmful gases such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxide. They also exclude toxic chemicals such as barium nitrate, lithium and cadmium found in traditional crackers. But they still emit smoke and PM, and are only marginally less harmful than traditional crackers. The apex court has, perhaps, overlooked the sheer volume of crackers that are burnt over the course of Dussehra and Diwali. Last year, a survey showed that the number of families bursting fire crackers rose 40 per cent over the previous year and half of them intended to burn traditional firecrackers alongside green ones. Even assuming that all consumers in the National Capital Region (NCR) are stricken by conscience and choose to burn only green firecrackers within the specified timings, the emission of PM10 and PM2.5 will still be high enough to create the characteristic post-Diwali haze compounded by unabated seasonal farm fires and low wind speeds.  It is possible that the Supreme Court has chosen a realistic path, given the cussedness of citizens who decline to cut back firecracker burning in the broader public interest. Since the popular discourse often centres on the right to freely practise religion, the court has stated that this right is not absolute. The court has balanced this right by invoking Article 21, the right to life and personal liberty, which the judges have interpreted as the right to a healthy, safe, and pollution-free environment. Outright bans have been spectacularly unsuccessful, so this via-media approach may assuage public and politico-religious sentiment. Even assuming the court’s diktat is followed, the burning of green crackers, which are, in fact, not so green, is unlikely to offer the NCR’s citizens a happy, pollution-free Diwali.   Topics : Supreme Court Diwali pollution Firecrackers Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: RBI should deepen financial markets rather than rely on restrictions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / RBI should deepen financial markets rather than rely on restrictionsRBI should deepen financial markets rather than rely on restrictions

The evolving global economic and financial conditions have resulted in significant volatility in the Indian financial market

premium

Reserve Bank of India (Photo: Reuters)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Nov 05 2026 | 11:40 PM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India (RBI) this week constituted a technical consultative committee for financial markets. It is expected to facilitate structured engagement with market participants and stakeholders on policy and operational issues relating to money markets, government securities, foreign-exchange markets, derivatives markets, and infrastructure. The committee, with most members drawn from outside the central bank, should help enable more informed intervention. Any such committee of experts that provides a forum for discussion involving market participants with the objective of improving the functioning of financial markets must be welcomed, particularly against the given backdrop.  The evolving global economic and financial conditions have resulted in significant volatility in the Indian financial market. While equity and bond markets have witnessed volatility over the past several months, the RBI’s focus has largely been on the currency markets. Although the rupee has gained over the past few trading sessions, it has been under considerable pressure, at least since the beginning of the Iran war. India faced the prospect of an increased current-account deficit along with persistent outflows on the capital account. The RBI also announced swap schemes to attract foreign flows and build buffers. It has used foreign-exchange reserves to stem the decline in the rupee. India’s foreign-exchange reserves have declined by about $66 billion from the record highs of $785.7 billion in the week ended September 4. It has also put various restrictions in the market for currency derivatives with a view to containing speculation.  It is in this context that the committee will have consultation with stakeholders. It is hoped that its deliberations and consequent RBI intervention will be made public for wider discussion. Notably, one of the terms of reference for the committee is: “Emerging policy and operational issues affecting financial markets, including implementation of RBI measures and identification of unintended market frictions.” This is a crucial aspect, and it would be interesting to know the views of the committee. One of the issues has been the level of central-bank intervention. As one of the experts pointed out on these pages recently, in 2025-26, the RBI bought government bonds worth about 2.5 per cent of gross domestic product, which was over 80 per cent of net central-government borrowing. This partly compressed government bond yields and reduced the yield difference with other markets, and may have affected capital flows. The RBI intervention was to improve liquidity, which got drained owing to foreign-exchange outflows and intervention in that market. More recently, the RBI was busy draining liquidity out of the market. Liquidity increased substantially with large inflows under the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits. The data shows that the RBI also had a net short dollar position worth about $240 billion in the forward market at the end of September. Clearly, it is trying to manage various things in the market.   It must be accepted that spillovers from global markets often complicate things in emerging-market economies. However, it must also be recognised that as India gets more integrated with the global economy, partly owing to new free-trade agreements, it will become increasingly difficult for the RBI to influence market outcomes without creating friction. For instance, last financial year, India exported goods and services worth over $850 billion, while imports stood above $950 billion. Thus, nearly about $2 trillion crossed the Indian borders in a year on just the trade account. Therefore, the need is to develop markets, not restrict them, and allow economic agents to take informed business decisions. The expert committee should be expected to draw up a fresh road map.   Topics : RBI Financial markets Foreign exchange reserves

entry.title: AI brings alive India's ancient knowledge through modern technology
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / AI brings alive India's ancient knowledge through modern technologyAI brings alive India's ancient knowledge through modern technology

AI, digital storytelling and manuscript digitisation are helping revive Indian mythology and ancient scientific knowledge, making cultural heritage more accessible to younger generations.

premium

AI and digital technologies are giving Indian mythology and ancient knowledge new reach, helping creators reinterpret epics for younger audiences while enabling researchers to study and preserve centuries-old manuscripts.

Pranjal Sharma3 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 5:54 PM ISTIn the festival season, technology is helping bring alive ancient stories, epic dramas and mythologies for a new generation of Indians.  Social media creators are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) and digital content tools to reimagine Indian mythology for younger audiences. AI-art storytellers use generative AI platforms such as Midjourney, DALL-E and Runway to create cinematic depictions of scenes from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, transforming ancient stories into visually rich reels and short videos. Mythology-focused influencers are also using motion graphics and visual effects to recreate legendary events such as the Kurukshetra war, Hanuman’s journey to Sri Lanka and Krishna’s teachings in ways that feel relatable and modern.  AI voiceovers, animated illustrations and digital avatars are being used to narrate lesser-known stories from the Puranas and regional folklore, making them more accessible to younger audiences. Other creators employ augmented reality filters that allow users to interact with mythological themes, characters and symbols through Instagram Stories and Reels. Animated creators, including those behind digital channels inspired by Amar Chitra Katha-style storytelling, are adapting traditional narratives into short, shareable video formats that blend historical interpretation with contemporary visual language.  The result is that ancient epics and mythologies are reaching millions of young Indians through immersive, technology-enabled storytelling. By combining AI-generated imagery, animation, special effects, audio technology and social media algorithms, influencers are helping keep cultural narratives relevant and engaging in the digital age.  Technology is also being used to examine and validate aspects of ancient Indian science by analysing historical texts, archaeological evidence, linguistic patterns and astronomical references. Researchers are applying machine learning and natural language processing to Sanskrit manuscripts, including the Vedas, Aryabhata’s astronomical works and Sushruta’s medical texts, to better understand historical dating and early empirical knowledge. AI tools are also helping scholars map astronomical observations described in ancient epics and compare them with modern celestial models.  Researchers at institutions including the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) have applied natural language processing to ancient mathematical, astronomical and medical manuscripts. This is making large collections of texts searchable and helping scholars identify scientific concepts systematically. The effort has revealed sophisticated treatments of grammar, mathematics and astronomy in works such as Aryabhata’s Aryabhatiya and Bhaskaracharya’s Lilavati.  A recent example is the use of AI and machine learning in Ayurgenomics, which combines principles from Ayurveda with modern genetics. The initiative has been highlighted by both the World Health Organization and India's Ministry of AYUSH as an example of AI being used to investigate whether traditional Ayurvedic classifications correlate with measurable biological and genetic traits.  This year, the Ministry of Culture's Gyan Bharatam initiative began piloting AI systems that can read, transcribe, search and analyse Sanskrit manuscripts on mathematics, astronomy, medicine and other traditional disciplines. These tools are helping researchers uncover, compare and validate scientific concepts buried in manuscript collections. IIT Bombay-based BharatGen is working with the ministry on an active pilot, building AI tools that help people read these texts, learn from them and recite them correctly.  Museums, libraries and archives are digitising manuscripts, paintings, photographs and ancient texts to prevent deterioration and make them widely accessible. Institutions such as the National Digital Library of India and the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts have created digital repositories containing millions of cultural artefacts. High-resolution scanning allows fragile documents, including palm-leaf manuscripts and rare books, to be preserved without repeated physical handling.  As AI advances, it is helping India understand its own heritage better. 
 The writer is an economic analyst and author.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Bharat Ratna LK Advani Ji at 100!
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Bharat Ratna LK Advani Ji at 100!Bharat Ratna LK Advani Ji at 100!

A former Deputy Prime Minister and one of India's longest-serving Home Ministers, Lal Krishna Advani Ji is one of the few people whose lives have touched many different chapters of modern India

premium

Senior BJP leader LK Advani turns 99 today, marking the beginning of his 100th year.

Narendra Modi New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 6:00 AM ISTShri Lal Krishna Advani Ji enters the hundredth year of his life today, November 8. This year, his birthday fittingly coincides with Diwali, a festival associated with Prabhu Shri Ram and the diya at a time when we are marking 75 years since the inception of the Jana Sangh, the 125th Jayanti of Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee, and recently celebrated a hundred years of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).   There are very few people whose lives have touched so many different chapters of modern India. Advani Ji was born on November 8, 1927, on Dev Deepawali. As a youngster in 1947, he experienced the pain of leaving behind his familiar world in Sindh. He rebuilt his life from scratch without bitterness. This trait of being able to build from scratch, against all odds, has stayed with him throughout. It was seen while he was strengthening the Jana Sangh and later building the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). His tenures as BJP President saw the Congress falling sharply from 400 to below 200 in 1989 and the BJP becoming the single-largest party for the first time in 1996. Advani Ji nurtured generations of karyakartas and gave the party a clear foundation rooted in the principle of ‘Nation First’.   Two qualities always set Advani Ji apart as a leader. First, his ideological clarity and intellectual sharpness. This was reflected in his speeches and writings. The Jana Sangh and BJP resolutions he authored remain worth reading even today, while his interviews were consistently incisive and precise. Second, the manner in which he exposed the pseudo-secularism propounded by a large section of the Indian polity for many years.    Advani Ji took up every responsibility with immense diligence. As an RSS pracharak, Advani Ji first worked in different parts of Rajasthan. From there, he went to the national capital, where he started working closely with Atal Ji. History shows that it is rare for two towering political leaders to work together for several decades, cooperating with each other without becoming competitors. Advani Ji and Atal Ji set a remarkable example. Together, they changed the course of Indian politics.  The Delhi that Advani Ji came to was coming to terms with the horrors of Partition. He immersed himself in making the Jana Sangh stronger. In 1967, Advani Ji became the Chairman of the Delhi Metropolitan Council, where he worked alongside the late Vijay Kumar Malhotra Ji (who became Chief Executive Councillor).   In 1970, Advani Ji’s Parliamentary innings began. His interventions have won appreciation across the political spectrum. He made a mark as an Member of Parliament (MP) and later, as Leader of Opposition in both houses and from the treasury benches, too. Despite Parliamentary commitments, he frequently travelled across India meeting people.    I vividly recall the 1991 Lok Sabha elections. It was decided that Advani Ji would contest the Lok Sabha elections from two seats, one of which was Gandhinagar. He had an old link with Gujarat. His father had settled in Kutch after Partition. Advani Ji had also served as a Rajya Sabha MP from Gujarat. So, it was a homecoming of sorts. Being involved in the BJP organisation, I had the honour of helping prepare his papers and assisting him throughout the campaign. The people of Gandhinagar sent him to Parliament time and again. As a voter of Gandhinagar, I also had the honour of voting for Advani Ji on numerous occasions. The care and attention he devoted to his constituency is something to learn from.   The Emergency was a watershed moment in Advani Ji’s life. He was at the forefront of saving democracy and protecting the Constitution. His experiences found their way into his book, ‘A Prisoner's Scrap-Book.’ One part of that book, titled ‘A Tale of Two Emergencies’, beautifully explained the striking similarities between the events in India starting June 1975 and those in Nazi Germany in 1933.   Advani Ji was a fiery Opposition leader but an equally excellent administrator. When the Janata Government came to office in 1977, Advani Ji became Minister for Information and Broadcasting. It is widely accepted that his work in this department was extremely impactful. As Deputy Prime Minister and one of India’s longest-serving Home Ministers, he was instrumental in strengthening India’s security apparatus. His work in improving the lives of our security forces is remembered with great fondness. His unequivocal stand against terrorism ensured India got a tough anti-terror law.   Of course, an iconic moment in Advani Ji’s life was the Somnath to Ayodhya Rath Yatra. It changed the course of Indian society for the better. I consider it a privilege that I got the opportunity to be involved in this yatra from the ideation stage to execution. Being present at Somnath when the yatra began was particularly special. A yatra can be very demanding, requiring long hours, constant travel, physical endurance and an ability to remain focused despite fatigue. Advani Ji embodied this endurance.  I also have memories of the saddening moments of Advani Ji’s arrest in Bihar. Then, in Gujarat, the BJP withdrew support from the Chimanbhai Patel government. With this, a simple message was given, that when it comes to our ideology and the Ram Temple, there will never be any compromise. Many of our senior leaders and karyakartas took an oath that, come what may, a Ram Temple will be built. And, years later, with the blessings of the people of India, a grand Mandir for Prabhu Shri Ram became a reality in Ayodhya.   There is so much more of Advani Ji that is outstanding. His simplicity, for example. After the Navnirman Movement, Advani Ji had come to Junagadh and stayed for a month as an ordinary karyakarta, preparing the party for the Assembly elections in which the Congress was rejected. He has always shown what probity in public life is about. He is a voracious reader. Those who have spent time with him know how carefully he goes through newspapers. He is a big fan of cinema and theatre, and has been an enthusiastic film critic. His sense of history and the need to preserve it is visible in his book, ‘My Country My Life’.  Advani Ji always remained in touch with Sindhi culture. Another effort he undertook was the popularisation of Sindhu Darshan Puja near Leh. I myself have been to one puja with Advani Ji and George Fernandes Ji.   Any account of Advani Ji’s remarkable journey would be incomplete without mentioning Kamla Advani Ji. She was a constant source of strength and support throughout his public life.  Growing up in Karachi, Advani Ji could hardly have imagined the path his life would take. In an expression of gratitude, the people of India conferred upon him the Bharat Ratna in 2024. As Advani Ji enters the hundredth year of his life, I pray that he be blessed with good health and that he continues to inspire us all as he has always done.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Narendra Modi LK Advani Bharat Ratna

entry.title: A 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultation
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / A 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultationA 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' test: Risks of reforms without consultation

Between the farm laws and Agnipath, you could say the Modi government erred in taking its most loyal constituencies for granted: Hindi-heartland farmers and soldiers

Representative Picture

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Nov 07 2026 | 11:53 AM ISTYou can find a more diplomatic or politically convenient description for it, but the Modi government’s latest move on the Agniveer scheme, brought in with such aplomb, is a rollback. More so, a poll-eve capitulation. Seventy-five per cent of the first lot of Agniveers would have finished their tour of duty, or walked the Agnipath (path of fire), as the scheme was named, and returned to their hometowns and villages by December. It’s just that many would have gone back to Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Punjab, even Manipur, all going to the polls this coming February. All are traditionally major catchment areas for armed forces recruitment. For the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the first two are much too vital to risk.  The prospect of these demobilised soldiers returning and joining opposition rallies, even enrolling in something like the Cockroach Janta Party, was scary for the BJP which, until the other day, was riding an all-conquering confidence. Now, it was seen as a risk not worth taking. On top of these, in November or thereabouts next year, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat will have their state elections. Gujarat, the BJP can still be calm about. But Himachal, a stronghold it lost to the Congress last time, is a traditional recruiting area with a large ex-servicemen’s constituency.

Also Read

 The party has now become far too risk-averse to put to the electoral test what was once its favourite reform. Reform it was, though. And we’ll talk about how, and then why it collapsed at its first test. There are three things governments are remembered for. Then there’s a fourth category: The good ideas a government implements and then withdraws under pressure or in panic. The good and the bad ideas are the first two. The third is the good ideas they propose but lack the nerve or skills to implement. We can list many of the United Progressive Alliance’s (UPA’s), for example: Aadhaar and India Stack based on it, direct benefit transfer (DBT) of welfare, even targeted delivery of subsidised cooking gas only to the poor and deserving. So were its many grand and audacious infrastructure projects of national importance. All got caught either in its indecision loop, internal party-versus-government contradictions, or ideological opposition. Most were subsequently consummated by the Modi government. Think the rail link to Srinagar, Mumbai Metro, Trans Harbour Link, the new Expressways, completion of the dedicated freight corridors (DFCs) and even the annihilation of armed Maoism. All of these were UPA projects abandoned midway. The Modi government did a brilliant job with these. It just tripped up on some of its own ideas. In journalism, we follow the three-example rule, meaning that these make a straight line. Or your argument. For Modi government’s rollbacks, count the farm laws, brought in with such self-assurance in 2020 and rolled back in their entirety in 2021 in the face of opposition from farmers. The second is now the Agniveer scheme. For the third, my preference would be the caste Census. The Modi government was opposed to it forever, then suddenly included it in the delayed 2021 Census being carried out now. This was under Rahul Gandhi’s pressure. If you don’t think that’s strong enough to make the third example —although I think it does, given the implications — I can give you another. The Prime Minister repeatedly derided the freebie culture, or what he contemptuously dismissed as “revdi” culture. Speaking at the inauguration of the Bundelkhand Expressway at Jalaun in UP in July 2022, he said, “This revdi culture is very dangerous for the development of the country. Those with revdi culture will never build new expressways, new airports or defence corridors for you.” And then, around the time of the Chhattisgarh elections in the winter of 2023, he announced that the Covid-era free food grain scheme would continue. In the same set of elections, the BJP brought in the Ladli Behna Yojana for cash transfers to women. Then, probably stung by the loss of majority in 2024, the party unleashed an almighty revdi “revolution”, with payouts reaching up to  ₹10,000 as a one-time transfer in Bihar and a promise of  ₹2 lakh if the woman started an enterprise. This was so expensive that even a rich state like Maharashtra is struggling to pay out, looking for excuses to reduce the number of beneficiaries. Women are already protesting, saying they’ve been denied their “Ladki Bahin” payouts. If you prefer, you can list this as the third example. However you look at it, this government has lost much of its appetite for risk, even with reforms where it had shown great conviction and commitment. These four examples are enough to show that the Modi government will also be remembered for the really good ideas it brought in, Agnipath included, and rolled back. This column, for the record, had supported each of these ideas. Between the farm laws and Agnipath, you could say the Modi government failed the test of both elements of the “ Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan” sentiment. It erred in taking its most significant and loyal constituencies for granted: Hindi heartland farmers and soldiers. The most disappointing thing is how it failed to reach out to them and build acceptance for such radical changes. People are by and large suspicious of major policy shifts with such significant implications for their lives, particularly when introduced through a shock-and-awe approach. That, however, has been this government’s style. Think sudden demonetisation or the Covid lockdown. Decisions affecting farmers and soldiers were taken in much the same way. Unlike the first two, which came with an end date, these policy changes were meant to survive in perpetuity. That explains the pushback from the base, and the Modi government’s rollback. Governance remains a painstaking, laborious, even boring business because it requires background work, scenario-mapping, war-gaming, or what the armed forces would call staff work. That is what the civil services and bureaucracies are there for. The absence of this precise element has bedevilled these plans — surprising, given how heavily the Modi government depends on civil servants. Were they asked to do their homework, or handed the decision first? There may be a concern that decisions could get caught in an analysis-paralysis loop. But you can’t always be like a commando who jumps out of a plane without checking the parachute. That isn’t fearless. It’s reckless. When Agnipath was implemented, it was well known that the first lot would leave on the eve of these state elections. An extensive rehabilitation programme, beginning midway through their four years, could have cushioned the blow. Now, the baby is gone, and with it the bathwater. The same lack of homework preceded the implementation of One Rank, One Pension (OROP). It was an election promise, all parties agreed with it, and no Indian would begrudge soldiers this benefit. But if the additional costs had been calculated and a necessary top-up provided to the defence budget, the story might have been different. The sudden increase in pensions because of OROP came from a defence budget that didn’t even keep pace with inflation over the years. This shrank the capital or acquisition budget. As concerns grew, Agnipath was rolled out in a hurry. Poor staff work created two kinds of soldiers, two sets of wages and even two sets of benefits for families in the event of a battle fatality. Most significant armies now have soldiers serving short tenures. But they don’t treat conscripted soldiers as a category separate from those on full-career service. Here, they were even addressed separately. Each unit then had an Agniveer sub-unit within it. This was unsustainable. The twin ideas of reducing the pension burden going ahead and making the armed forces much younger were both virtuous. Both have been lost to poor planning, hasty implementation and now withdrawal. This first batch will finish its sixth year on the eve of the 2029 general election. Rescuing this good idea will be a political miracle. It’s looking like a case of na khuda hi mila, na visaal-e-sanam (neither did I find God, nor my beloved).

entry.title: Why cutting capital gains tax may not bring foreign investment to India
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Why cutting capital gains tax may not bring foreign investment to IndiaWhy cutting capital gains tax may not bring foreign investment to India

Income should be taxed on the same principle, whether it comes from labour or capital beyond ideology

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Jagannathan6 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 10:44 PM ISTThe finance minister has indicated the government’s willingness to re-examine India’s long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax on equity, driven largely by the need to attract foreign investors at a time when the rupee and the balance of payments (BoP) are under pressure. It should do no such thing. Our capital gains tax regime is broadly on the right trajectory, with tax rates on gains from different types of assets converging. The case for re-examining what is essentially a good thing is very weak, especially when capital gains taxes remain a significant source of revenue in a difficult year.  There are two parallel areas of reasoning to note here. One relates to the medium-term pressure on the BoP and the rupee in an environment where global interest rates are high and specific sectors like artificial intelligence (AI) are sucking up huge amounts of capital away from emerging markets like India. The other relates to the principles that should govern taxation of incomes arising from capital investments.  Let’s deal with the first issue here — the short- to medium-term pressure on the BoP resulting from outflows of foreign portfolio capital, mainly from the stock markets. Many foreign investors are leaving not because India is a bad story, but because the medium-term prospects for growing their money seem better elsewhere. This outflow, which is being accentuated by the weakness in the rupee despite a massive $140 billion inflow through foreign-currency non-resident (bank) deposits, or FCNR (B), and external borrowings, is worrying the government and the central bank. Administrative measures have been taken by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to prevent excessive speculation and foreign exchange hedging, and oil companies have been given a separate window outside the regular market for foreign exchange purchases. But the weakness continues. The government has also reduced to zero the tax on interest earnings from government securities for foreign investors, which makes sense, for these can be negative-return avenues when the currency is depreciating.  These are good things to do in the short term, but cutting LTCG on equity investments is not just a tactical move. It has long-term implications for both domestic and foreign investor sentiment, not least because we are now changing the rules for arbitrary reasons. In any case, there is no reason to believe that a cut in or the elimination of LTCG tax will actually bring in more dollars, as some foreign investors could well decide that zero LTCG means they can carry their gains out of India for investment in US Treasuries. More so, when they know that this is being done to ease the pressure on the rupee, and could be reversed later. There is no certainty that a tax cut will bring in the dollars rather than prompt investors to take their gains and run.  As a country with a large gap between domestic savings and investment, we need foreign capital, but the right way to attract it is not by cutting capital gains taxes. There is no substitute for making India a long-term and safe bet for patient investors who want to build manufacturing or services entities in this country. This has to be done by making it easier for them to invest here, and not just making it easier for them to exit faster. A blow-hot-blow-cold approach to tax policy will hardly reassure them that policies are stable for the long term. If taxes can be cut on a whim, why can’t they be reintroduced on a whim too?  This brings us to the principles that should underlie taxation of incomes on invested capital. Capital investments generate three basic types of incomes for the investor — interest, dividends, and capital gains. The Modi government has tried to bring dividends on a par with income earned from labour by abandoning the old dividend distribution tax (DDT), which was essentially payable at the corporate end and did not differentiate between dividends paid to a small shareholder and those with large holdings. Essentially, it indirectly taxed small shareholders and benefited large shareholders, including promoters. In parallel, the Modi government raised taxes on earnings from investments in debt to bring them on a par with bank deposits, while also abandoning the tax-free bonds scheme, which again was a benefit only for those in the highest tax brackets.  LTCG rates were raised in the 2024 Budget, and most capital gains on multiple assets were taxed at 12.5 per cent, plus surcharge, where applicable, for higher income earners. Put simply, taxes on dividends were treated on a par with income earned from other sources, while taxes on equity capital gains were treated preferentially. This makes sense to some extent, as equity is risk capital, and India needs risk capital to boost productivity and growth.  One can see the thought behind various changes. The government has been slowly equalising taxes on income from debt and income from salaries and other forms of labour, while keeping taxes on capital gains on favourable terms. Keeping LTCG at a relatively low level compared to taxes on interest, dividends, and income from labour work is probably justified in order to attract risk capital, but zero tax on capital gains? Is there any better way to silently send the message that capital needs to be mollycoddled more than labour, when we have millions needing jobs?  A cut in LTCG can be done in two ways: One, by restricting it to foreign investors, or, two, by making it available to all investors. I don’t think the domestic investor is demanding any such sops for herself, when systematic investment plans are drawing such huge inflows. Why should the government pander only to foreign investors, who are here only for the profits and nothing more? There is a case for not discriminating against hot flows, but certainly not for discriminating against locals to favour foreign investors. An exception can perhaps be made for debt investments, where the rupee’s weakness can deter foreign investors, but not domestic ones.  The principle of taxing incomes should be the same whether one earns it from labour or capital investment. The case for a reasonable differential between taxation of risk capital and labour is probably well-established, but not for a lopsided preference for treating equity with kid gloves.  A strong case for abolishing LTCG tax can be made only when the country decides to abolish income taxes altogether or offers very high tax-free thresholds. For what we are really taxing here is income. Where that income comes from does not matter all that much. And if a cut in LTCG is being considered as a short-term tactical move, like the FCNR (B) gambit, why not say that only equity investments made between now and March 31, 2027, will qualify for these zero rates? But even that is not a good idea, for it complicates the tax regime further — which is not a worthwhile move when we are trying to simplify things. So, no, don’t mess with LTCG.

entry.title: How India's finance brands turned the 'Bhabhi' into a trusted voice
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / How India's finance brands turned the 'Bhabhi' into a trusted voiceHow India's finance brands turned the 'Bhabhi' into a trusted voice

From the intimidating bank manager to the trusted Bhabhi, finance has found a new face

premium

Sandeep Goyal5 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 10:39 PM ISTFor 40 years, finance in India had a face. It was a man, 48 years old. In a suit. With a moustache. And glasses that said, “I know more than you.” He sat behind a big wooden desk at a public-sector bank. He spoke in English that you didn’t fully understand. He made you feel small. He made you feel like you had come to ask for a favour, even if it was your own money.  That was finance. Father-like. Strict. Distant. “Beta, form bhar ke laao. Kal aana.” Then, quietly, finance got a sex change. Finance is no longer your father. Finance is now your Bhabhi. And that is the biggest marketing shift in BFSI (Banking, Financial Services and Insurance) in the last decade.  Open any finance ad today. Who is talking? It’s not the suit-man. It’s a warm, smiling, 32-year-old woman in a salwar suit, or a saree, who says, “Arre, SIP toh main bhi karti hoon. Bohot easy hai. Chalo main samjhati hoon.” That’s Bhabhi.  She is not your mother — mothers are too emotional. She is not your wife — wives are too direct. She is not your girlfriend — girlfriends are too risky for finance. She is Bhabhi. The perfect Indian balance. She is your elder, so you respect her. She is family, so you trust her. She is approachable, so you can ask her stupid questions. She will not judge you if you don’t know what mutual fund means. And every financial brand in India has hired her.  HDFC Bank — For 20 years, its ads looked like Aditya Puri in a suit. Now? Its last five campaigns have a young woman in the kitchen, explaining that a personal loan is not a big deal. “Aapka ghar, aapka loan.” The Bhabhi who manages the house budget better than the husband.  SBI YONO — The app that your father found intimidating. Who sells it now? Not the manager. A daughter-in-law in an ad, telling her father-in-law, “Papa, YONO pe FD ho jayegi, aapko branch jaane ki zaroorat nahi.” The Bhabhi has reversed the power. She teaches the older man.  ICICI Prudential — All their mutual fund ads are now Bhabhis. Not experts. “Main apne bachche ke liye SIP karti hoon.” It’s not return, it’s responsibility.  Even the bad boys did it.  Cred — Started with Rahul Dravid as Indiranagar ka gunda, Jim Sarbh, all male cool. What happened? No one understood what CRED does. So they brought in Bhabhi. Now their Instagram is full of women creators explaining, “CRED pe rent pay karne se kya hota hai.” The male cool didn’t convert. The Bhabhi explanation did.  Zerodha — Nithin Kamath is the coolest finance bro in India. But who is actually bringing in Tier 2 women investors? His videos with his wife Seema Patil, and creators like Shreya Kapoor, and Neha Nagar. The language changed from “bullish-bearish” to “dekho, ye stock aise samjho jaise sabzi mandi.”  Why did this happen? Because men ruined finance. For 30 years, we made finance about fear and ego. “You don’t know. I know. So listen to me.” The result? We created a country that saves in gold, under the mattress because gold doesn’t ask for a PAN card.  Finance had a trust deficit, not a knowledge deficit. And trust, in Indian families, doesn’t come from father. It comes from Bhabhi. In every Indian home, who do you go to if you need ₹10,000 urgently without telling anyone? Bhabhi. Who knows your real salary, your real debt, your real gold? Bhabhi.  Who explains your father’s complicated medical report in simple language? Bhabhi. So, finance did the smartest thing. It fired the suited man and hired the Bhabhi.  This is not just about ads. It’s a product strategy.  > SIP is a Bhabhi product. Small, monthly, no big risk, like a kitty. ₹500 per month. Father would have said, “₹5 lakh ka lump sum lao.” Bhabhi says, “₹500 se shuru karte hain.”  > Gold loans are now Bhabhi-fied. Muthoot’s old ads were tough Malayali men with moustaches. Now Manappuram’s ads have Madhuri Dixit saying, “Gold is yours, loan is easy.” She is India’s most loved Bhabhi.  > Insurance is Bhabhi-fied too. LIC’s old ads were about death. HDFC Life’s ads are about “Sar Utha Ke Jiyo” — but explained by a wife to her husband.  The language has changed too. From “wealth creation, portfolio diversification, asset allocation” to “bachche ka future, thoda thoda, chalo saath mein dekhte hain.”  From English to Hindi to Hinglish. From return to responsibility. From fear to care.  Namaste Bhabhi!

entry.title: Amid Karnataka Congress tensions, a leadership test for DK Shivakumar
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Amid Karnataka Congress tensions, a leadership test for DK ShivakumarAmid Karnataka Congress tensions, a leadership test for DK Shivakumar

The strongest Congress government in Karnataka in 37 years looks to be its weakest

premium

Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar

Aditi Phadnis5 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTThe Congress won 178 seats of the 224 in the Karnataka Assembly elections in 1989, exactly when the party lost power at the Centre after its stupendous victory five years earlier. And the Karnataka record is unbeaten till today. Veerendra Patil was credited with that victory and he became chief minister. But following communal riots and Patil’s failing health, Rajiv Gandhi removed him, replacing him with S Bangarappa and later Veerappa Moily. It was Mr Moily who led the Congress into the 1994 Assembly polls and it got just 34 seats.  The short point of this statistical overload is that it takes very little to turn spectacular victories into historic defeats. Many think the current Congress government in Karnataka is headed in that direction again.  In the 2023 Assembly elections, the Congress won 135 seats on its own. It was a handsome victory. The party only needed 113 to form the government. Siddaramaiah became chief minister amid rumours that he had committed himself to handing over power to then deputy chief minister D K Shivakumar in 30 months.  That “agreement” had to be enforced by the high command. M Siddaramaiah stepped down in bad grace, and gave way to Mr Shivakumar, considered both resourceful and efficient. But that reputation has unravelled sooner than expected. Today, the strongest Congress government in Karnataka in 37 years looks to be its weakest.  To be fair, not all of the blame should fall on Mr Shivakumar. When the state-run milk cooperative brand Nandini increased milk prices by ₹8 a litre a few days ago (prices of butter and ghee going up was inevitable), it was only following other milk cooperatives across the country. The chief minister pleaded with the cooperative to reduce the increase in curd prices, which it did. But this might have been a tactical mistake. It suggested he had the power to intervene in pricing but was choosing to limit it to curd.  Objective financial reasons also led to the announcement of a 23-35 per cent increase in state-run bus fares last week. Transport Minister Byrathi Suresh told the Legislative Council in September that the four state-owned road transport corporations (RTCs) had posted an annual loss of ₹8,000 crore because of four consecutive increases in the prices of diesel and other petroleum products by the Centre. But women travel on these buses free as part of the Congress’ 2023 poll promise (the Shakti scheme). So, in popular perception, men have been cross-subsidising the fares of the women all along and at the end of the day, the government is recovering its money via a fare elevation so it’s done no one any favours by enabling women to travel free. In fact, the state government reimburses the state transport corporations for the losses incurred by the Shakti scheme. That the state transport corporations are inefficient and corrupt is another story. But in politics, explaining niceties isn’t always easy.  When you add to that the outcome of a sting operation on Siddaramaiah, the current chief minister’s stock falls further. A Congress activist, Kripa Alva, claimed to have a clip showing Siddaramaiah engaged in crimes against minors. The chief minister ordered an enquiry and Ms Alva was expelled from the party but not before Opposition leader H D Kumaraswamy, also a Union minister, alleged that the video clip was released at the behest of the chief minister, whose reputation as the “King of Stings” has spread far and wide. Mr Kumaraswamy’s message is: The Congress is at war with itself. There seems to be no counteroffensive from the state unit of the party. On the contrary, state party chief, B K Hariprasad, has said he is doubtful how fair the enquiry will be since political leaders are involved.   All this is telling on Mr Shivakumar’s famed management skills. The Congress lost all four seats in the recent Legislative Council polls. It isn’t that he doesn’t have efficient colleagues. The minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Krishna Byre Gowda, is both hardworking and result-oriented. Health Minister U T Khader is known for his calmness and delivery though he became a minister only in June. As minister for industries and infrastructure development, M B Patil is the man behind investment in Karnataka. But political and resource management is ultimately Mr Shivakumar’s responsibility.  The only consolation for the party is that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) seems to be in a lethargic slump. State chief B Y Vijayendra’s term ends on November 10, and despite the party’s performance in the Council elections, his detractors in the party believe he might be between jobs. There seems to be little effort to hit the streets: The BJP’s wars against the government are being fought on social media.  It might be time for Mr Shivakumar to stop, take a deep breath and re-centre himself and his government. Assembly elections are due in the summer of 2028. If he has to pull a rabbit out of a hat, the time is now.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: CR7 heads out: Ronaldo leaves behind a legacy beyond goals and records
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / CR7 heads out: Ronaldo leaves behind a legacy beyond goals and recordsCR7 heads out: Ronaldo leaves behind a legacy beyond goals and records

Fans will long squabble over whether Messi or Ronaldo is entitled to the 'greatest of all time' accolade... this is a pointless exercise

premium

Cristiano Ronaldo

Kanika Datta5 min read Last Updated : Nov 06 2026 | 10:19 PM ISTIn 2003, Manchester United, which lorded over the English Premier League with eight titles and one Champions’ League trophy till then under Alex Ferguson’s forceful stewardship, played a friendly match against Portuguese club Sporting CP. They lost 3-1, but it was the post-match developments that proved decisive for an 18-year-old Cristiano Ronaldo.  He wasn’t on the scoresheet that day, but his dribbling skills and ability to read the game had already caught Sir Alex’s eye. It was the senior Man U players who clinched the decision for him.  On the bus and plane ride home, they badgered their manager — no mean feat given his legendary temper — to sign the teenager. They were pushing at an open door; with the team’s celebrated no. 7, David Beckham, headed for Real Madrid, Man U needed a comparable replacement fast.  Even before he proved himself on the pitch, Ronaldo, sporting a kooky hairstyle and ear studs, made headlines, with Man U paying Sporting CP £12.4 million, a record-breaking sum at the time. Rivals Liverpool and Arsenal, also in the race, dropped out, saying they valued the player at about a quarter that sum. The rest was not just history for Man U — which went on to win three more Premier League titles and one Champions League trophy with him — but for Ronaldo, too. He bagged the first of his five Ballon d’Or awards before going on to a stellar career in Real Madrid and Juventus. He drew a slavish fan following, not just from the teams he represented but neutral and opposition fans as well. Who will forget how the entire stadium stood up to applaud his bicycle kick goal in the 2018 Champions League match against Juventus?    Now, as he hangs up his studs from international football at the ripe age of 41, older heads will judge his retirement as long overdue. Indeed, younger fans who never had the privilege of watching CR7, as his fans called him, in his prime would have wondered what the fuss was all about had they watched his dismal performance in the recent World Cup. Where his great rival Lionel Messi walked and jinked around opposition defenders for Argentina, Ronaldo was a shadow of himself, unable to execute those incredible jumps that earned him the record for the most headed goals in football history (158) or make those darting runs into the box to score the 985 goals of his career. Yet just 10 years before, he powered Portugal to a Uefa Euro trophy, the nation’s first major tournament title, with three goals (all critical ones) and two assists. In the final against France, he was forced off  with knee injury after a cynical tackle. But in a show of inspired captaincy he ran up and down the sidelines — which his manager, marooned in a mandatory technical area, could not do — bellowing instructions and encouragement to his team until a little-known substitute called Eder drove in a goal from a distance to win Portugal the match.    Retiring from international football within a month of each other, fans will long squabble over whether Messi or Ronaldo are entitled the “Greatest of All Time” (GOAT) accolade. As with the Roger Federer versus Rafael Nadal debate in tennis, this is a pointless exercise. One scored more goals (Ronaldo: 985; Messi: 937). The other had more assists (Messi: 428; Ronaldo: 261). One had more Ballon D’Ors (Messi: eight; Ronaldo: five) … and so on and so forth. But as with Federer and Nadal, to reduce Messi and Ronaldo’s careers to stats is to do them a disservice. Both gave fans hours of sheer delight and both contributed to the development of football as we know it in unique ways.  Much has been written about how Messi, who retired on October 6 at age 39, conserved his energy by walking between 40 and 60 per cent per match. Ronaldo represented the new age of iron discipline and fitness that is demanded of top level footballers. Where Diego Maradona, drank and drugged his way through a dazzling career at the age of 33 (though it was over long before that), Ronaldo ate and drank with the fastidiousness of a fashion model. As Sir Alex admiringly wrote in his book Leading, as Ronaldo aged, he kept himself underweight in the interests of agility and speed. Though he would occasionally be photographed with his arm around a “young lady” (Sir Alex’s  words) in a night club, he drank only water and slept early.  If there was a difference between the two greats, it was in their lifestyles. Where Messi has a burnished reputation as a family man ever faithful to his childhood sweetheart, Ronaldo has been dogged by allegations of rape; his attempts to pay for the victim’s silence did not enhance his personal standing. The latter’s contract with the shady Saudi club Al Nassr, which includes influencer fees quite apart from how he performs on the pitch, and a Nike sponsorship deal ensures that he will out-earn Messi by several millions. That, too, is a feature of modern football superstardom. This generation of emerging greats will stand on their shoulders.
